lessons.title: Crude oil, alkanes and cracking
lessons.summary: Find out what crude oil is, how fractional distillation separates it into useful fractions, the properties of alkanes, and how cracking turns long hydrocarbon chains into fuels and alkenes.
objectives: I can describe crude oil as a finite mixture of hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes, and write the formulae of the first four alkanes.
I can explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil using differences in boiling point.
I can describe how the properties of hydrocarbons change with chain length and write equations for complete combustion.
I can explain why cracking is carried out and balance cracking equations.

activities.title: What is crude oil?
activities.content:
## Crude oil: a mixture from ancient plankton

**Crude oil** is a thick, dark liquid found trapped in rocks. It formed over **millions of years** from the remains of tiny sea creatures and plants (plankton) that were buried in mud, then squeezed and heated in the absence of oxygen. Because it takes so long to form, crude oil is a **finite resource**: once it is used up it cannot be replaced on any useful timescale.

Crude oil is not one substance. It is a **mixture** of a very large number of compounds, almost all of which are **hydrocarbons**.

A **hydrocarbon** is a molecule made of **hydrogen and carbon atoms only**. Watch that word *only*: ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is not a hydrocarbon because it contains oxygen.

Most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil belong to a family called the **alkanes**. Being a mixture matters because the different compounds are not chemically bonded together, so they can be separated by a physical process. That process, fractional distillation, is the next part of the lesson.

Crude oil is the raw material for **fuels** (petrol, diesel, kerosene) and for a huge range of **feedstock** chemicals used to make plastics, solvents, lubricants and detergents.

activities.title: The alkanes
activities.content:
## Alkanes: the simplest hydrocarbon family

Alkanes are a **homologous series**: a family of compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties, where each member differs from the next by a CH₂ unit.

The general formula for an alkane is:

$$C_nH_{2n+2}$$

So if you know the number of carbons, you can find the number of hydrogens. The first four alkanes are ones you must remember:

| Name | Formula | Number of carbons |
|---|---|---|
| Methane | CH₄ | 1 |
| Ethane | C₂H₆ | 2 |
| Propane | C₃H₈ | 3 |
| Butane | C₄H₁₀ | 4 |

A memory aid for the prefixes: **M**onkeys **E**at **P**eanut **B**utter (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-).

Alkanes are **saturated** hydrocarbons. This means every carbon atom is joined to its neighbours by **single covalent bonds only**; there are no double bonds and no room to add extra atoms. In a displayed formula each carbon shows four bonds, and the hydrogen atoms fill all the spare positions.

Alkanes are fairly unreactive apart from burning, which is exactly why they make good fuels.

question.text: An alkane molecule contains 8 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it contain?
question.hint: Use the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 8.
question.explanation: H = 2n + 2 = (2 × 8) + 2 = 18. The alkane is octane, C₈H₁₈.

activities.title: Fractional distillation
activities.content:
## Separating crude oil

The hydrocarbons in crude oil have different **boiling points**, and that difference is used to separate them in a tall **fractionating column**.

1. The crude oil is **heated** until most of it **evaporates**, and the vapours are fed into the bottom of the column.
2. The column is **hot at the bottom and cooler at the top**, so there is a **temperature gradient**.
3. Vapours rise. Each hydrocarbon **condenses** back to a liquid when it reaches the height where the column temperature falls below its boiling point.
4. Liquids are collected at different heights as **fractions**. A fraction is a group of hydrocarbons with **similar boiling points** and similar chain lengths.

### Where each fraction ends up

| Position in column | Fraction | Chain length | Boiling point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top | Refinery gases (LPG) | Very short | Lowest (still gases) |
| Upper | Petrol, naphtha | Short | Low |
| Middle | Kerosene (jet fuel), diesel | Medium | Medium |
| Lower | Heavy fuel oil, lubricating oil | Long | High |
| Bottom | Bitumen (for roads) | Very long | Highest |

**Short chains** have low boiling points and rise to the **top**. **Long chains** have high boiling points and condense near the **bottom**; the very longest never evaporate at all and drain out as bitumen.

Exam answers should mention: heat, evaporate, temperature gradient, condense at different heights, similar boiling points.

activities.title: Worked example: properties and chain length
activities.content:
**Why does the length of a hydrocarbon change its properties?**

Longer molecules have **stronger intermolecular forces** between them (more surface for the molecules to attract each other). More energy is needed to pull them apart, which explains the trends below.

| Property | Short chain (e.g. butane) | Long chain (e.g. C₃₀H₆₂) |
|---|---|---|
| Boiling point | Low | High |
| Viscosity (how thick / gloopy) | Low, runny | High, treacle-like |
| Flammability | Very easy to ignite | Hard to ignite |
| Volatility (ease of evaporating) | High | Low |

**Applying this:** A student is asked why petrol is used in car engines but bitumen is used for roads.

*Petrol* has short chains, so it is **volatile** and **highly flammable**: it vaporises easily in the engine and ignites readily. *Bitumen* has very long chains, so it is **viscous**, hard to ignite and stays solid at road temperatures, which is exactly what you want under a car tyre.

The trick is to name the property **and** link it to the use.

question.text: Which statement correctly describes hydrocarbons with longer carbon chains compared with shorter ones?
question.hint: Think about how thick and how flammable heavy fuel oil is compared with petrol.
question.explanation: Longer chains have stronger intermolecular forces, so they have higher boiling points, are more viscous and are less flammable.

options.text: Higher boiling point, more viscous, less flammable
Higher boiling point, less viscous, more flammable
Lower boiling point, more viscous, less flammable
options.feedback: Longer chains need more energy to separate, so they boil at higher temperatures.

options.text: Lower boiling point, less viscous, more flammable

activities.title: Combustion of hydrocarbons
activities.content:
## Burning hydrocarbon fuels

When a hydrocarbon burns with plenty of oxygen it undergoes **complete combustion**. The carbon is oxidised to **carbon dioxide** and the hydrogen is oxidised to **water**. Energy is released, which is why we burn fuels in the first place.

$$\text{hydrocarbon} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$$

For methane:

$$CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O$$

### Balancing a combustion equation

1. Write the formula of the hydrocarbon, O₂, CO₂ and H₂O.
2. Balance the **carbons** first: one CO₂ for each C.
3. Balance the **hydrogens** next: one H₂O for every two H.
4. Count the oxygens on the right, then balance O₂ last (you may need a half, which you can then double everything to remove).

For propane, C₃H₈:
- 3 carbons → 3CO₂
- 8 hydrogens → 4H₂O
- Oxygen on the right: (3 × 2) + 4 = 10, so 5O₂

$$C_3H_8 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 3CO_2 + 4H_2O$$

Combustion is an **oxidation** reaction: both carbon and hydrogen gain oxygen. If there is not enough oxygen, incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide and soot, which you will meet in the atmosphere topic.

question.text: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of butane by filling in the missing numbers.
question.hint: Two butane molecules contain 8 carbons and 20 hydrogens. Balance C, then H, then O.
question.explanation: 8 carbons → 8CO₂. 20 hydrogens → 10H₂O. Oxygen needed on the right: 16 + 10 = 26, so 13O₂.

activities.title: Cracking
activities.content:
## Making the fractions we actually want

Fractional distillation gives us more long-chain fractions than anybody wants, and fewer short-chain fractions such as petrol than we need. **Cracking** fixes that. It breaks **long-chain alkanes** into **smaller, more useful molecules**: shorter alkanes (good fuels) and **alkenes**.

Cracking is an example of a **thermal decomposition** reaction (breaking down using heat).

### Two methods

| Method | Conditions |
|---|---|
| **Catalytic cracking** | Hydrocarbon vapour passed over a hot **catalyst** (e.g. a zeolite / aluminium oxide) at about 500 °C |
| **Steam cracking** | Hydrocarbon vapour mixed with **steam** and heated to a **very high temperature** (over 800 °C) |

### The products

A cracking equation always has **one long alkane** on the left and **an alkane plus an alkene** (sometimes more than one) on the right. The atoms must balance.

$$C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_8H_{18} + C_2H_4$$

### Why alkenes are valuable

Alkenes contain a **C=C double bond**, which makes them far more reactive than alkanes. They are the starting material for **polymers** (plastics) and many other chemicals. Alkenes react with orange **bromine water**, turning it **colourless**; alkanes do not. That test lets you tell the two apart in the lab.

There is also strong **demand** for cracking because short-chain fuels sell for more than the heavy fractions they come from.

activities.title: Worked example: completing a cracking equation
activities.content:
**Dodecane, C₁₂H₂₆, is cracked to make octane, C₈H₁₈, and one other product. Identify the other product.**

The atoms on each side must balance.

- Carbons: 12 on the left, 8 in octane, so the missing molecule has 12 − 8 = **4 carbons**.
- Hydrogens: 26 on the left, 18 in octane, so the missing molecule has 26 − 18 = **8 hydrogens**.

The other product is **C₄H₈**, which is butene, an alkene (it fits CₙH₂ₙ).

$$C_{12}H_{26} \rightarrow C_8H_{18} + C_4H_8$$

**A second example with two alkenes:** hexadecane, C₁₆H₃₄, cracks into octane (C₈H₁₈) and **two** molecules of one alkene.

- Remaining carbons: 16 − 8 = 8, split into two identical molecules gives 4 carbons each.
- Remaining hydrogens: 34 − 18 = 16, giving 8 hydrogens each.

$$C_{16}H_{34} \rightarrow C_8H_{18} + 2C_4H_8$$

Check: alkanes fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and alkenes fit CₙH₂ₙ, which is a quick way to confirm your answer makes sense.

question.text: Which TWO of the following are reasons why cracking is carried out?
question.hint: Think about which fractions are in demand and which reactive molecules are useful for making plastics.
question.explanation: Cracking converts less useful long-chain fractions into short-chain fuels that are in higher demand, and produces alkenes which are used to make polymers. It does not create crude oil and does not separate mixtures.

options.text: To make more short-chain fuels, which are in higher demand than long-chain fractions
To produce alkenes, which are used to make polymers
To separate crude oil into fractions
options.feedback: That is fractional distillation, a physical separation.

options.text: To turn alkenes into alkanes

question.text: Put these fractions in order of where they are collected in a fractionating column, from the TOP down to the BOTTOM.
question.hint: The shortest chains with the lowest boiling points rise highest.
question.explanation: Refinery gases have the shortest chains and rise to the top; petrol next; kerosene in the middle; bitumen has the longest chains and drains from the bottom.

question.text:
Crude oil is separated into fractions in an oil refinery.

(a) Describe how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions. (3 marks)

(b) One fraction contains hydrocarbons with about 30 carbon atoms. Explain why this fraction is collected near the bottom of the column. (1 mark)
question.hint: Use the key words: heated, evaporate, temperature gradient, condense, boiling point.
question.explanation: (a) The crude oil is heated so that it evaporates, and the vapours enter a column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. The vapours rise and each hydrocarbon condenses at the height where the temperature is just below its boiling point, so fractions with similar boiling points are collected at different levels. (b) Long chains have strong intermolecular forces and high boiling points, so they condense near the hot bottom of the column.

markScheme.criterion: Crude oil is heated / evaporated / vaporised
Column has a temperature gradient: hotter at the bottom, cooler at the top
Hydrocarbons condense at different heights according to boiling point
Long chains have high boiling points so condense near the bottom

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Crude oil** is a finite mixture of hydrocarbons (hydrogen and carbon only), mostly **alkanes**.
- Alkanes: general formula **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**, saturated (single bonds only): methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀.
- **Fractional distillation**: heat, evaporate, temperature gradient, condense at different heights, fractions of similar boiling points.
- Longer chains → higher boiling point, more viscous, less flammable, less volatile.
- **Complete combustion**: hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (oxidation).
- **Cracking** (catalytic or steam) breaks long alkanes into shorter alkanes (fuels) + **alkenes** (for polymers); alkenes decolourise bromine water.

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these substances is a hydrocarbon?
practiceQuestions.hint: A hydrocarbon contains carbon and hydrogen atoms only.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Propane, C₃H₈, contains only carbon and hydrogen. The others contain oxygen or chlorine as well.

options.text: C₃H₈
C₂H₅OH
options.feedback: Ethanol contains oxygen, so it is not a hydrocarbon.

options.text: CO₂
CH₃Cl

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: crude oil is a renewable resource because it is still forming today.
practiceQuestions.hint: How long does crude oil take to form?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Crude oil takes millions of years to form, so on any human timescale it is finite and non-renewable.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Match each alkane to its molecular formula.
practiceQuestions.hint: Count the carbons from the prefix: meth = 1, eth = 2, prop = 3, but = 4.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀; each fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the word equation for the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon.
practiceQuestions.hint: Carbon and hydrogen are both oxidised.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.

practiceQuestions.text: Decane, C₁₀H₂₂, is cracked to form propene, C₃H₆, and one alkane. How many hydrogen atoms are in a molecule of the alkane produced?
practiceQuestions.hint: Subtract the atoms in propene from the atoms in decane.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Carbons: 10 − 3 = 7. Hydrogens: 22 − 6 = 16. The alkane is heptane, C₇H₁₆, so 16 hydrogen atoms.

practiceQuestions.text: A liquid hydrocarbon is shaken with orange bromine water and the mixture stays orange. What does this show?
practiceQuestions.hint: Which family of hydrocarbons reacts with bromine water?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Alkenes decolourise bromine water because of their C=C double bond. No colour change means the hydrocarbon is saturated: an alkane.

options.text: The hydrocarbon is an alkane
The hydrocarbon is an alkene
options.feedback: An alkene would have turned the bromine water colourless.

options.text: The hydrocarbon has been cracked
The hydrocarbon contains oxygen

practiceQuestions.text: Describe the conditions used for catalytic cracking of a long-chain hydrocarbon.
practiceQuestions.hint: The hydrocarbon has to be a gas, and it needs something to speed the reaction up.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The hydrocarbon is heated so that it vaporises, and the vapour is passed over a hot catalyst (such as aluminium oxide or a zeolite) at a high temperature of around 500 °C.

markScheme.criterion: Hydrocarbon is vaporised / heated to form a vapour

practiceQuestions.text: Put these hydrocarbons in order of increasing boiling point (lowest first).
practiceQuestions.hint: Longer chains have stronger intermolecular forces.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Boiling point rises with chain length: methane (1 C), butane (4 C), octane (8 C), C₂₀H₄₂ (20 C).

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO statements about alkanes are correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the type of bonds in an alkane and its general formula.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated (single C–C bonds only) and fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. They do not have double bonds and do not react with bromine water.

options.text: They contain only single carbon–carbon bonds
They have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
They turn bromine water colourless
They each contain at least one C=C double bond

practiceQuestions.text:
An oil company finds that fractional distillation gives it far more heavy fuel oil than it can sell, but not enough petrol.

(a) Name the process the company can use to convert heavy fuel oil into petrol and describe what happens to the molecules. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why the alkenes produced by this process are useful. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: The process breaks long chains into shorter ones. Alkenes have a double bond that makes them reactive.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Cracking breaks down long-chain alkane molecules by thermal decomposition into shorter-chain alkanes (used as petrol) and alkenes. (b) Alkenes are reactive because of their C=C double bond and are used as the starting materials for polymers and other chemicals.

markScheme.criterion: Long molecules are broken down into shorter alkanes and alkenes
Alkenes are reactive because of the C=C double bond
Used to make polymers / plastics / other chemicals

practiceQuestions.text: A student writes the formula of an alkane that contains 26 hydrogen atoms. How many carbon atoms are in one molecule of this alkane?
practiceQuestions.hint: Alkanes fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Set 2n + 2 equal to 26 and solve for n.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 2n + 2 = 26, so 2n = 24 and n = 12. The alkane is dodecane, C₁₂H₂₆.

practiceQuestions.text: Pentane (C₅H₁₂) and eicosane (C₂₀H₄₂) are both alkanes found in crude oil. Which row correctly compares pentane with eicosane?
practiceQuestions.hint: Pentane has the much shorter chain. Think about what short-chain fuels such as petrol are like.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pentane has a shorter chain, so the intermolecular forces between its molecules are weaker. It therefore boils at a lower temperature, is runnier (less viscous) and catches fire more easily than eicosane.

options.text: Pentane has a lower boiling point, is less viscous and is more flammable
Pentane has a lower boiling point, is more viscous and is less flammable
Pentane has a higher boiling point, is less viscous and is more flammable
options.feedback: Shorter chains have weaker intermolecular forces, so they boil at lower temperatures.

options.text: Pentane has a higher boiling point, is more viscous and is less flammable

practiceQuestions.text: Balance the equation for the complete combustion of pentane by filling in the missing numbers.
practiceQuestions.hint: One pentane molecule has 5 carbons and 12 hydrogens. Balance C first, then H, then count the oxygens on the right.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 5 carbons → 5CO₂. 12 hydrogens → 6H₂O. Oxygen atoms on the right: (5 × 2) + 6 = 16, which is 8O₂. C₅H₁₂ + 8O₂ → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O.

practiceQuestions.text: A refinery passes vapour from its heavy fuel oil fraction over a hot catalyst. Which TWO statements about the products of this process are correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: Cracking is a thermal decomposition. Think about the size of the products and which family of products contains a double bond.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cracking breaks long alkane chains into shorter alkanes, which are useful fuels, and alkenes, which contain a C=C double bond and are used to make polymers. The products are smaller, not larger, and cracking is a chemical reaction rather than a separation by boiling point.

options.text: Shorter-chain alkanes are produced that can be used as fuels such as petrol
Alkenes are produced that can be used to make polymers
The hydrocarbons are separated according to their boiling points
options.feedback: Separating by boiling point is fractional distillation, not cracking.

options.text: Longer-chain molecules are built up from the heavy fuel oil
options.feedback: Cracking breaks molecules down; it does not build them up.

practiceQuestions.text: Four fractions leave a fractionating column at different heights. Put them in order from the BOTTOM of the column up to the TOP.
practiceQuestions.hint: The longest chains have the highest boiling points and condense lowest down, where the column is hottest.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Lubricating oil has the longest chains of the four and is collected lowest. Diesel is next, then naphtha, and refinery gases (LPG) have the shortest chains and leave from the very top.

practiceQuestions.text:
A sample of crude oil contains hexane (C₆H₁₄, boiling point 69 °C) and hexadecane (C₁₆H₃₄, boiling point 287 °C).

(a) Crude oil is described as a mixture of hydrocarbons. State what is meant by the term **hydrocarbon**. (1 mark)

(b) Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why hexadecane has a much higher boiling point than hexane. (2 marks)

(c) In a fractionating column, state where hexane will be collected compared with hexadecane and give a reason. (1 mark)
practiceQuestions.hint: A hydrocarbon contains only two elements. Longer molecules attract each other more strongly. Low boiling point vapours rise further before they condense.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) A hydrocarbon is a compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only. (b) Hexadecane molecules are much longer, so the intermolecular forces between them are stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them, giving a higher boiling point. (c) Hexane is collected higher up the column than hexadecane because its low boiling point means it stays as a vapour until it reaches the cooler upper part of the column.

markScheme.criterion: Hydrocarbon: a compound of hydrogen and carbon only
Hexadecane molecules are longer / larger so intermolecular forces are stronger
More energy is needed to overcome these forces / separate the molecules
Hexane is collected higher up because its boiling point is lower so it rises further before condensing
